calNow: Cal has said no to his father with his own hands and lied to a theater board for a friend who never asked. He has a professor who sees through him, a partner who read him whole, and a father waiting on Thursday with a blazer that carries an old stain. Someone is watching his window at 3:07 a.m., and Yusuf is closing in.

cast.name: Dev Okafor
cast.impression: The nicest guy on campus and the one who has your back. You finally told him 'My father made a call. That's the whole lottery'; he'd known since Brooks said 'Daddy's single' and was waiting for you to say it. He quizzed you on the Rho roster with flashcards, took the Brooks clip on the chin ('It's fine. It's funny.'), and asked you not to ask about Tuesday: 'I'll tell you this one day.' The coin and the envelope are still unexplained; you let him go.

cast.name: Priya Raman
cast.impression: Your self-appointed emergency contact, fast, funny and still not eating. She waited the hour and four more asleep against your door and covered with a joke; you carried her to bed. You paid the hour at her callbacks (she's Nina now), sat outside the bathroom door talking and she slept on your shoulder. She doesn't know you saw her pages and vouched for her show. On camera she rages that someone hurt Dev. You said 'We're ok. Always.'

cast.name: Nora Castellanos
cast.impression: Sharp, fair and now your editing partner. Her Monday piece called you 'the Whitaker problem' and noted you paid for her coffee. In Marsh's room she told the table she lied to her abuela about eating. You handed her your essay; she read every page and said 'That's somebody's life. It's yours,' then struck your coffee debt off her list. Her covered corkboard and her own essay stay closed.

cast.name: Margaux Vance
cast.impression: Marble in daylight, someone else after dark, and for one afternoon, in glasses. You finally answered 'Who'd you call?' by text ('My father. I called my father. I was eleven'), and she took you to a library to say 'Mine would have let it ring.' You kissed her in daylight and a librarian saw. She said 'Until it doesn't, we don't' about the photographer. Away from you, someone is leaning on her to be seen with you, and she is refusing.

cast.name: Danny Doyle
cast.role: High-school junior · Busboy at Dot's Diner
cast.impression: A seventeen-year-old busboy with a pencil behind his ear and a side hustle. You bought what he was selling; a stranger at the Rho door recognised his work and called him an artist.

cast.name: Richard Whitaker
cast.impression: Cal's father, still never on camera. His assistant forwards your mail, and he sent his own old Rho blazer with a card: 'Mine. Thursday.' He texts 'Econ. Not poetry' and 'Proud of you.' When you stay in English he says 'We'll discuss it Thursday.'

cast.name: Simon Achterberg
cast.impression: Your self-appointed guardian: certificate of wardship in hand, Sunday visitation observed, camel coat, Lillet. He is repeating Marsh's seminar and was thrilled for you. He tells you to find out who your father was before he was your father, starts to ask about Richard's twenties, and stops: 'Ailment of mine.' He went quiet at the mailroom ('You're building a file on your own father').

cast.name: Yusuf Haddad
cast.impression: Dev's roommate: eleven words a day, all of them devastating. He traced the account to the third-floor wifi, kept it from Dev, and asked permission before going further. You said yes; he said 'Tomorrow.' He is on your side and wary of what he finds.

cast.name: Brooks Hadley III
cast.role: Junior · Sigma Kappa Rho pledge master
cast.impression: The Rho's pledge master: beautiful, easy, with a laugh you half-recognise and a tell that mirrors your own. He seems to know things you told only one person and quotes your father's private words back at you. He made you swim in the dark, and shook when you came back. He likes you, he is using you, and he said you only get one good insult. He texts you homework: the 1991 roster, 'Now learn the names.'

blocks.text: Each bubble lands a few seconds after the last, with a little hitch between them, the rhythm of somebody typing while they walk. Walking where, at nine minutes past three, he doesn't ask himself. He is very good at not asking himself things. He has been practicing all week.

He looks down through the bay window. The Quad is floodlit and empty, the paths pale as bone, the grass black in the middle where the lights don't reach. At the top of the Commons steps, eighteen inches tall, his grandfather's name, lit like a stage nobody is on.

3:14. At the end of the hall the stairwell door sighs on its closer. Slippers, soft and fast on the old carpet, the way you walk when you're trying to be a rumor. Two doors down, a door clicks shut very carefully, the way you close a door on a sleeping baby. Or a crime.
He opens his own door.

The hallway is empty and red under the exit sign. Down the middle of the carpet, from the stairwell to the door with the fairy lights, runs a trail of dark, damp prints in the shape of slippers. And here and there in them, pressed into the pile, blades of cut grass. Bright green. Fresh. The Quad's grass, from the middle of the Quad, where the lights don't reach. Exactly where you'd have to stand to photograph his window.
Five days ago he carried her down this hallway in her duvet, and she pretended to be asleep, badly. Now he could follow her footprints up it.
He said sorry to her on this carpet on Friday.
He lied to her on this carpet on Friday. She let him.

The prints are already fading at the edges, drying from the outside in, the way everything on this floor does. Gerald ticks. Nobody else is awake to see it. Except, two doors down, behind the fairy lights, somebody very much is.

choices.label: Knock on her door. Softly.

reaction.text: One knuckle, the way you knock on a hospital door. Thirty seconds. Then her door opens a hand's width: duvet, Kevin the skull under one arm, eyes far too bright for someone who was asleep.
I was asleep.
Her slippers are dark to the ankle. He looks at them. She watches him look at them.
Gerald. He spills.
Night, Nina.
Night, Konstantin.

The door closes. He stands in the red light long enough to hear her not move on the other side of it. Neither of them goes to bed for a while. They just stand there, a door apart, both perfectly still, like two people waiting for a photograph to finish.

choices.label: Text her: ‘Your slippers are wet, Raman.’

reaction.text: Read 3:15 AM. The dots come and go four times, like someone trying keys in a lock.

Then nothing. Through the wall two doors down he hears her laugh once, high and wrong. Then her door, and the slippers again, and the tap in the bathroom at the end of the hall, running for a long time. He lies down on his mattress and listens to it run, and doesn't get up, and hates exactly how good he's getting at that.

choices.label: Photograph the footprints. Close the door.

reaction.text: He crouches in his boxers and photographs the carpet: the prints, the grass, the line of them running from the stairwell to her door. The way he photographed the empty oval. The way he photographed Mrs. Pell's filing card. The collector.

Then he shuts his door and sits on the floor against it, the phone in his hand. Two photos now, one on top of the other: his window from the grass, and the grass in the hallway. The same night from opposite ends.
He doesn't sleep. Gerald, for once, has nothing to add.

INT. CAL'S SINGLE, LOWELL HOUSE. MORNING (WED 7:30 A.M.)
Cal is awake because he never went to sleep. He's on the floor mattress in yesterday's T-shirt with the Moleskine on his chest like a cat that has decided not to move.
A knock. Two knuckles, precise, like a man testing a melon.
Yusuf Haddad in the doorway: hood up, laptop under one arm, two cups of Commons coffee balanced in the other hand in a way that suggests engineering.
You said yes. Yes comes with coffee.
You said you knew. Now I do too.
You said no. I looked anyway. It looked at Dev first.
Across the hall, through two doors and a shower curtain, Dev Okafor is singing gospel in the shower. Badly. With total commitment. It's a song about a river, and he is losing to the river.
Yusuf sits on the edge of the mattress without being asked, which is the most physically familiar thing he has ever done, and opens the laptop on his knees.

blocks.paren: glancing down at the mattress on the floor
blocks.text: At least you can't build that crooked.
Tomorrow.
A beat.
Today.
He says the rest like weather.
The three-oh-seven post was different. The others are scheduled. That one went up live. From a phone, on cellular. From the Quad. Middle of the grass. You can tell from the angle of the Commons sign.
You can tell that from a sign?
It's eighteen inches tall. It's very consistent. Then the same phone joined the Lowell wifi. Third-floor access point. Three-fourteen.
Phones introduce themselves when they join a network. They say their names. It's very polite.

He turns the screen. A list of devices, times, a column of little green dots. Hunters-iPhone. JUNE RA DO NOT. DOCTOR-dev. And one line, at 3:14, with a yellow Post-it stuck over it on the screen, the sticky edge lined up exactly with the row, like a bandage on a paper cut.
I put a Post-it on it. In case you want to keep not knowing. People are allowed.
Cal hands him his own phone without a word: the carpet, the slipper prints, the blades of grass. Yusuf studies it like a slide under a microscope.
Grass. Good. Analog confirmation.
Secret lottery.
It's the running joke. This morning it's the kindest thing anyone could say, and they both know it.
From across the hall Dev hits a note that should be illegal in Massachusetts. Yusuf doesn't look up. One finger rests on the edge of the Post-it, not pressing.
Cal doesn't need to read under it. That's the trouble with reading people: you do it whether you want to or not, and by the time somebody offers to show you the page, you already have it by heart.

choices.label: Ask Yusuf to peel it off: ‘Show me.’

reaction.text: Yusuf peels the Post-it off with one finger and sticks it to his own knee.
priyas-iphone. Lowercase. No apostrophe. Like a whisper.
Cal looks at it for a long time. Yusuf looks at the wall. In the shower Dev reaches the river's far bank and sounds very proud of himself.
I'd rather not have had to. I told you. Things I find find me back.
He closes the laptop, leaves both coffees on the floor, and stops at the door without turning around.
Dev doesn't know. Dev won't know from me.

choices.label: ‘I know whose it is.’

reaction.text: Yusuf doesn't move the Post-it. He looks at Cal for the first time all morning: the full look, the one that takes inventory and counts the spoons.
Then why haven't you said anything?
You still haven't said anything.

Cal has no answer that isn't a lie, so he gives none. Yusuf nods as if that's an answer too. He closes the laptop with the Post-it still stuck to the screen, so it'll be there when he opens it, like a bandage nobody's allowed to take off.
You should say something. Before something else gets posted.

choices.label: ‘Delete it. Don't tell Dev.’

reaction.text: I don't delete things. I stop looking. It's different. Deleting is a lie about the past. Not looking is just a decision about the future.
He closes the laptop with the Post-it still on. At the door he stops.
Dev's going to find out. Dev finds out everything. He just doesn't say.
Then, the most words Cal has ever heard him volunteer:
He'd want to hear it from you. Not from a Post-it.

INT. PRUITT HALL, THIRD-FLOOR CORRIDOR. DAY (WED 8:55 A.M.)

The lake in the window is the color of a nickel. Twelve partner drafts on the scarred oak table, face-down, like a card game nobody wants to start. The assignment was a phone call. For Cal it was the call.
Partners. Swap. Read. Don't be kind. Kindness is a form of not reading.

He slides Nora the pages he copied out of the Moleskine at dawn, onto yellow legal paper, in his best handwriting, which is still bad. She slides him one typed page. Before he can turn it over she says, not looking up:

He dropped her class. He comes anyway, at 8:55, with his pages folded in thirds, and slides them under Marsh's office door like a ransom note. Then he stands in the corridor outside Seminar Room 3 and listens through the wall to a room he isn't in. At 10:50 the door opens, twelve people come out, and one of them stops in front of him.
Partners was the assignment. You're still mine. Marsh said.
She hands him one typed page. Then, before he can turn it over:
I know I'm good.
His text, last night: Read it twice. You're good.
Twice?
Twice.
Who reads a newspaper twice.
Me, apparently.
The tips of her ears go faintly pink, and she looks furious about it, as if her ears have leaked to the press.

He turns her page over.
A call to her abuela's kitchen in Queens, before she was born.

“The phone rang in my abuela's kitchen in ██████. My father answered because he was the oldest one home. He was ████████. The voice said ███ ██████████ ████. The voice said ████████ ██ ███. The voice said ██████.”

The rest is the kitchen: a bolero on the radio, a pressure cooker hissing like it knows something. And one line in the clear: Every year after, she set a plate for him at the table, and every year nobody sat there, and every year she washed it anyway.
Three coats of black marker, edge to edge. A fence, built post by post.
Miss Castellanos. A redacted draft is still a draft. Barely.
It's a seminar on unreliable narrators. I'm withholding.
Withholding is allowed. Lying isn't. Know which one you're doing.
Nora reads his pages fast, like someone who already knows the house and is only checking the rooms.
You put the motel's name in. Good. Names are load-bearing.
Okay.
Okay.
Your first lie's in here. Third paragraph. You didn't flag it.
He looks. Third paragraph. He can't find it, which is what makes it the first one.

Then Marsh is behind his chair. He didn't hear her come. She reads over his shoulder, his handwriting on the legal pad: I said, Dad, she's not sleeping. He said, Where are you. She taps the page once with a short, unpainted nail.
Whose voice is missing from this call?
Mine.
No.
She walks on. She doesn't explain.
This is one sentence, Mr. Whitaker. A call has two ends.
This is one sentence, Mr. Whitaker. A call has two ends.
He reads Nora's page again. The bars. The plate. He reads what people leave out for a living. She knows it. She handed it to him anyway.

Then, a beat later, because he asked and didn't push:
Yet.

She looks startled to have said it. She takes his pages back and writes something across the top in green pen, and covers it with her forearm, and doesn't let him see it until the end. When he finally does, it says: Second sentence is better than the first. Write the third.

reaction.text: He writes it small, in pencil, beside the first bar, and hands the page back. She reads it. She reads it again, the way he read her article, and her mouth does the thing it did on move-in day when she refused to laugh at him.
She writes underneath his line, in green: Noted.
Then, on top of his pages: Second sentence is better than the first. Write the third.
It's the nicest thing anyone has written on anything of his. It's also an assignment. With her, those turn out to be the same thing.

reaction.text: He lifts her page to the gray window like a kid checking a twenty. Nothing. Not a letter. Not a ghost of one.
Three coats. I know who I'm partnered with.
Simon, across the table, applauds silently with two fingers.
Mr. Whitaker, the light is for reading. Not for burglary.
The table laughs, and Nora almost does, and catches it, and puts it away somewhere for later. On top of his pages, in green: Second sentence is better than the first. Write the third.

blocks.text: INT. WHITAKER COMMONS DINING HALL. DAY (WED 12:40 P.M.)
Lunch, alone, by choice, at the far end of a long table under his grandfather's portrait, which watches him eat soup like it's about to ask what he's done with the money.

On his way out of Lowell this morning he passed the Herald's THE WHITAKER PROBLEM, still taped to the bulletin board by the stairs. Somebody has added a lipstick heart over his name. He doesn't know whose lipstick. This week he has started wanting to know whose everything.
His phone. MARGAUX (DON'T). The first thing she's sent since Bring nothing.

He reads it three times. Saturday she wrote Your floor has a photographer. Until it doesn't, we don't. Last night the photographer posted his window at 3:07 a.m. As far as he can tell, nothing has changed except, apparently, her mind.
Twice now he's told her a true thing about his father. She's the only person he does that with. He doesn't know if that's why she's asking, or why he wants to go.
The last time she let him see her in daylight, a librarian coughed like a gunshot.
The last time she let him see her in daylight, she showed him a building made of glass.
The last time she let him see her in daylight, she asked him to make the account stop.

blocks.text: INT. THE GRIND, WHITAKER COMMONS. DAY (WED 4:00 P.M.)

The coffee bar off the Commons lobby, under the second, smaller portrait of Charles Whitaker, the one over the espresso machine, where he looks like a man who'd tip badly. The window table is the one every path on the Quad goes past. You can't sit there by accident. Nobody ever has.

Margaux is already in it. Full daylight armor: camel coat, hair like a decision, no glasses. Two tables over, three Kappa sisters are pretending to study a single organic chemistry textbook. One of them lifts her phone and doesn't pretend.
Margaux doesn't look at them. She looks at him, and at the chair, and he sits in it.

She has ordered for him. The right thing: oat flat white, extra shot, which he has never once told her. For herself, a small black drip, the cheapest thing on the board. When the barista calls the second drink she goes to the counter and pays for it in exact change from a little leather coin purse, quarters, dimes, a nickel, her fingers fast and practiced, like someone who has done this many times when nobody was looking.
Margaux Vance. Counting quarters.
She comes back and sees him seeing it.
I hate tipping on a card. It's vulgar.
You told me the truth about your father on a lawn. I'm returning the favor in a coffee shop. It's very modern.
She isn't wearing his parka. He notices she isn't, and that's how he knows she still has it.
The Kappas know there's a boy. They've known since the sweatshirt. The phone two tables over is how they're learning which one.

She asks him nothing about his father. Not Convocation, not Trustee Weekend, not one of the little list questions she used to ask like she was reading them off a card. She asks about the seminar. She listens to the answer. When he tells her about Nora's black bars and Marsh's dead fern, she laughs once, at exactly the right place: the real laugh, the one from the dark, by day, in public, while a girl two tables over films it.
Outside the glass, the Quad goes by. Two rowers. A tour group. A boy in a Rho quarter-zip who slows down, looks, and speeds up again with his phone already out.
Don't look at them. They're not the audience. They're the ushers.

choices.label: ‘Whose idea is this?’

reaction.paren: instantly, smoothly, looking him dead in the eye
reaction.text: Mine.
It's the most perfect sentence she has ever said to him, and something in its perfection snags, like a sweater on a nail. He can't find the nail. He just feels the pull.
You want it to be someone else's. So you don't have to like it.
She finishes the drip in one swallow, like medicine.
I liked it.
She goes. Through the window he watches her cross the whole Quad without looking back once, which, he realizes, is its own kind of being looked at.

reaction.text: He does it slowly, so she can stop him. She doesn't. Her hand is cold from the window glass and doesn't move in his. Then it turns over, palm up, which is a different thing entirely.
The phone two tables over gets all of it.

She doesn't let go until her coffee's cold, and then she lets go all at once, like a person stepping off a curb.

reaction.text: You're not watching me. You're watching her phone.
Margaux's smile holds. And the coin purse, he doesn't say, and she hears him not say it. It's in the air between them like the steam off the cups.
Everyone's seen on purpose, Cal. You of all people. You toasted your absent father to three hundred phones.
A beat.
Thank you for not saying the other thing.
She leaves a nickel on the table for the busboy, exactly, and her hand is not quite steady putting it down.

I deliver good news in person and bad news by email. It's policy.
She stops at the fairy-lit door and knocks twice. Priya opens it in a towel turban with a highlighter in her teeth.
Board voted. Six-one. Spring solo slot. The Boy Across the Hall.
Board voted. Six-one. Spring solo slot. The Boy Across the Hall.
Board voted. Four-three. Spring solo slot. The Boy Across the Hall. It was close. It was ugly. You won.

Priya screams so loud that June comes out of her room holding a hot glue gun like a revolver. Priya hugs Mae, who stands there with her arms at her sides like a coat rack being hugged by weather. Dev comes out of the double with his DOCTOR sleep mask pushed up on his forehead. Hunter, from the bathroom doorway, does a single calf raise in celebration.
Then Hunter swoons sideways into the radiator in a very specific imitation of Cal's Konstantin, and Gerald clanks in protest, and the whole hall cheers.

You said. It's not a thing. It's a symptom.

And she's gone down the hall with her phone to her ear, calling somebody, or nobody, shrieking “SIX-ONE” at a voicemail greeting.
He watches her spin and knows, and the knowing sits in his chest like a swallowed stone.

Same minute, across campus. Kessler Rink at six in the morning is a cold that gets into your fillings, the sweet chemical breath of the Zamboni, a single row of lights out of four, and the scrape and boom of captains' skate echoing off a roof built for three thousand people who aren't here.
In the stands: one spectator. Cal Whitaker, in a hoodie, with two coffees, because he said I'll be there, and for once in his life he is.
The captain is still out of town; the seniors are running it, which mostly means yelling. On the bench, a tired assistant trainer with a tablet and a whistle he doesn't use.
Tommy Reyes sees him from center ice and loses his mind.

My locksmith came!

He skates over and pounds the glass with a glove, sunglasses pushed up on top of his helmet like a tourist at a ski lodge. Cal holds up the second coffee. Tommy presses his face to the plexiglass and makes a sound like a seal receiving a fish.

blocks.text: Big day, hon. Rush!

The Lowell table by the windows. Dev with eggs. Yusuf with toast. Simon in a fresh scarf. Hunter with a protein shake the color of a swimming pool. At 7:04 every phone at the table stays dark. Nobody says anything. Then Hunter checks his. Twice.

blocks.name: HUNTER
blocks.text: Huh. The account didn't post.
The account is gone, darling. Deleted in the night. I have a source. My source is that I refresh it hourly. It's a sickness. I'm seeing someone about it.

blocks.name: HUNTER
blocks.text: Gone gone? Like, who was it? Was it June? I always thought it was June.
Hunter, if I knew, I'd be insufferable. I'm only regular sufferable.
Everyone looks at everyone. Dev cuts his egg.

At 7:06 Priya walks in wearing Tommy's spare sunglasses, the pair he left on the ficus last night, gets no food, and sits down directly across from Dev. She takes the sunglasses off. And she says it. The whole thing, July to last night, in under a minute, to his face, in a low steady voice, while the table pretends very hard to be talking about lacrosse.
Dev listens to all of it. He doesn't look away once.
Okay.
A beat.
Did you eat?
She doesn't answer. He pushes half his toast across the table to her. She looks at it like it's a contract.

Priya slides in next to Cal at 7:06, wrecked and bright, in yesterday's mascara and a fresh sweater, and steals the toast off his plate and holds it for the entire meal without eating it, like a prop in a scene about breakfast.
Priya's chair is empty. On it, her Nina script from last night's run-through, dog-eared, with a Post-it stuck to the cover in purple marker: SAVE MY SEAT (JK).

blocks.paren: to the table, to his egg
blocks.text: Everybody's telling the truth at breakfast this week. It's a lot.

Through the tall windows the Quad is filling with freshmen in navy, practicing handshakes on each other like boxers shadowboxing. RUSH, says a banner on the Commons steps, under his grandfather's name. Somebody has already turned the S into a dollar sign. Somebody always does.
Cal's phone buzzes.

msgs.text: A Rho boy called my son's room a charity.
You tell them his mother is a CPA.

blocks.text: Yusuf is watching him over his toast. Yusuf knows whose account it was. Simon knows only that it's dead. Hunter knows nothing. And the whole table is eating around a hole in the shape of a girl.
Yusuf is watching him over his toast. Yusuf knows whose account it was. Simon knows only that it's dead. Hunter knows nothing. And the whole table is eating around a hole in the shape of a girl.
Yusuf is watching him over his toast. Everybody at this table heard every word, and everybody is eating as if they didn't, carefully, around a hole in the shape of a girl who is sitting right there.

choices.label: Sit beside her chair. Whatever's in it.

reaction.text: He sits next to her. She bumps his shoulder once, the way he bumped Dev's on Mill Street the first night, and doesn't look at him, and doesn't stop holding the toast.
He moves around the table and sits next to her, across from Dev. Under the table, her knee is going like a sewing machine. He puts his own against it until it slows.
He sits next to the empty chair. He moves the script onto his lap, so nobody puts a tray on it, and keeps it there for the whole meal, like a coat he's holding for someone in the bathroom.
Yusuf watches him do it and eats a whole piece of toast, which for Yusuf is a sonnet.

choices.label: Sit with Dev. Say: ‘I knew. Since yesterday morning.’

reaction.text: He gets up, goes round to Dev's side of the table, and says it low, under the roar of Hunter's blender, while Priya is busy holding her toast hostage. Nobody else is meant to hear.
He gets up, goes round to Dev's side of the table, and says it low, under the roar of Hunter's blender. Nobody else is meant to hear.
Dev doesn't look up from his egg.
Since before that. You watched her on Monday like she was a test you'd already seen the answers to.
He pushes the hot sauce across without being asked.
It's fine.

And this time he doesn't make it sound like it's funny. He just makes it sound like it's fine, which from Dev is a much bigger thing, and also much smaller, and Cal can't tell which, and Dev is not going to help him.

choices.label: Take your tray to the Grind. Eat alone.

reaction.text: He gets up without a joke, which on the third floor is a press release.
At the Grind, under his grandfather's smaller portrait, he eats a blueberry muffin in four bites and reads the rush schedule Denise sent in August. THURSDAY · NIGHT ONE · LEGACIES. ATTIRE: FAMILY.
He reads the word FAMILY four times. It doesn't get any bigger. It doesn't get any smaller either.

blocks.text: INT. WHITAKER COMMONS DINING HALL. MORNING (THU 7:04 A.M.)

blocks.name: LORRAINE
blocks.text: Big day, hon. Rush!
7:04, and nothing chimes, because the account is gone, and the silence at the Lowell table is louder than any post ever was.

Priya isn't there. LOWELL 3 (NO RAS) is at 214 unread messages. June has called an emergency floor meeting for eight tonight, “with snacks, Hunter,” in a message with four separate exclamation points, which for June is a scream.
Dev doesn't sit next to Cal. He sits across from him, which he has never once done. It's a small thing. It's a whole continent.
Dev sits where he always sits. He hasn't touched his eggs. Dev, who sat on the hall carpet outside her door until three.
Dev sits where he always sits. He hasn't touched his eggs. Hunter says he saw Dev on the carpet outside her door at three, just sitting.
Simon arrives with the full intelligence briefing, sunglasses on his head, unwrapping a scarf like a bandage.
Varga knows. Varga does not care. Varga says, and I quote, “Chekhov stole from everyone.” Your friend keeps Nina.
Your friend keeps her place in the ensemble. Varga said, “The ensemble is where we put sinners.”
Also: I'm not to discuss the floor. I've been asked. By myself. I'm breaking it now.
Tommy comes in late from the rink, still damp, sunglasses on, scrolling his phone at last, and stops dead in the middle of the aisle with a tray of six waffles.
Wait. WAIT. The account was RAMAN? She cast me as a peasant!
Wait. WAIT. The account was RAMAN? She cast me as a peasant!
Wait. WAIT. The account was RAMAN? So who made me verified?

blocks.name: HUNTER
blocks.text: Nobody made you verified, bro.
Somebody made me SOMETHING.

blocks.name: HUNTER
blocks.text: She cast all of us, bro. I was Trigorin.

blocks.name: HUNTER
blocks.text: She cast all of us, bro. I was Trigorin.
You were AVAILABLE. I was a PEASANT.
You were AVAILABLE. I was a PEASANT.
Nobody laughs. Yusuf eats one triangle of toast in total silence, looking at Cal the whole time, chewing like a man reading a verdict.

Through the tall windows the Quad is full of freshmen in navy, practicing their handshakes on each other. RUSH, says a banner on the Commons steps, under his grandfather's name. Somebody has made the S into a dollar sign. Somebody always does.
He was right. In public. Everybody at this table agrees he was right. They're just eating around the hole it left, carefully, the way you eat around a bone.

choices.label: Ask Dev: ‘Should I not have?’

reaction.text: Dev takes so long to answer that Simon stops talking, which is a medical event.
You should have. Just not like that.
Then, because he's Dev:
You want the hot sauce?
Cal takes it. He doesn't want the hot sauce. It's the kindest thing on the table, and he puts it on eggs that don't need it, and eats them, because Dev is watching.

choices.label: Fill a tray. Take it up to her door.

reaction.text: Toast. A banana. A yogurt. The easy things, the things nobody has to decide about. He carries it up three flights and sets it on the carpet outside the fairy lights, and knocks once, and goes.
When he comes back an hour later for his bag the tray is still there, untouched. Somebody has drawn a smiley face on the banana in black Sharpie.
He doesn't know if that was her or Hunter. He'll never know. It's the not-knowing he'll keep.

choices.label: Eat. Say nothing. Read the rush schedule.

reaction.text: He eats like a Whitaker: fast, upright, looking at his phone. THURSDAY · NIGHT ONE · LEGACIES. ATTIRE: FAMILY.
That's the face your dad makes. On the business channel.
Nobody laughs. Yusuf didn't mean it as a joke. Yusuf has never once in his life meant anything as a joke, which is what makes him so funny, and so not, this morning.

blocks.text: INT. WHITAKER COMMONS DINING HALL. MORNING (THU 7:04 A.M.)

blocks.name: LORRAINE
blocks.text: Big day, hon. Rush!
7:04. Nothing chimes.

blocks.name: HUNTER
blocks.text: No post? Lame. I had a theory it was gonna be about rush.
I got four DMs about the clip. Strangers. People are nice. Kind of.

Across from Cal, Priya has a bagel she isn't eating. At 7:04 exactly she checks her phone under the table, the way you check a pulse. Her face does something small and private: a frown. A scroll. A second, deeper frown.
She looks up. At Cal.
He's looking at his eggs. They're very interesting eggs. He has never in his life been so interested in eggs.

He can feel the exact weight of her attention on the side of his face, the way you can feel sun through a window. He knows that look. He invented that look. He has been aiming it at people across tables since he was eleven, and he never once wondered what it was like to sit in it.
Yusuf is looking at both of them, chewing nothing. His look is the look of someone who knows that Cal knows, and is waiting to see how long Cal can carry it.
Yusuf is looking at both of them, chewing nothing. His look is the look of someone who knows that Cal knows, and is waiting to see how long Cal can carry it.
Yusuf pointedly isn't looking at either of them. He's looking at his toast as if it's a ceasefire.
Simon is talking about the smoker's dress code, which he has obtained from a source and which he describes as “Connecticut, but in mourning.”
Weird. Instagram's being weird.
Weird. Instagram's being weird.
Instagram logged me out of something. Rude.
Instagram is a mood disorder with a logo.

blocks.name: HUNTER
blocks.text: My Instagram's fine. I post my lifts.
And we're all so grateful.

Priya laughs at that, a perfect laugh, the curtain-call laugh. Her eyes don't leave Cal's face while she does it. She's reading him the way he reads everyone, and for the first time all week he understands what that's like from the other side, and it's like standing in a window at three in the morning with the lights on.

choices.label: Play innocent: ‘Something wrong, Nina?’

reaction.text: Nope!
The voice she used on her mother through his closet door. She puts the phone face-down. She takes a bite of bagel, a real one, and chews it for a long time, looking at him.
He holds her eyes. His thumb doesn't go to his eyebrow.
He's getting better at this. That's the problem.

choices.label: Look at your eggs.

reaction.text: He studies his eggs like they're a text from someone he's afraid of. Across the table she studies him studying them.

The whole table goes on talking about blazers and ties and whether Hunter can wear lacrosse shorts to a smoker (“It's September, it's basically summer, it's basically the beach”), and underneath it two people say nothing at all, in a language nobody else at the table speaks.
Yusuf picks up his tray and leaves. He has never once left first.

choices.label: ‘Maybe it's a sign. Log off for a day.’

reaction.text: She goes still.
It's a perfectly normal sentence. It's also the cruelest thing he has ever said with a smile, and they both hear it, and nobody else at the table does, which makes it worse.
Maybe. Maybe I will.
She leaves the bagel. She leaves the table. She doesn't look back, and her walk to the tray return is very straight, very even, like someone on a balance beam.
To logging off. The only true luxury.

blocks.text: INT. CAL'S SINGLE, LOWELL HOUSE. DAY (THU 4:00 P.M.)
The rush hours. The afternoon goes by like a waiting room with a fish tank in it.
4:02 p.m. Email. DENISE FARROW. Subject: Tonight!!
“Hi Cal! Your father will call you at 7:30 to discuss your schedule before the smoker! He's between dinners so keep it brief. No worries! -D.”
“Cal, your father will call you at 7:30 to discuss your schedule before the smoker. He's between dinners, so please keep it brief. Best, Denise.”
“Cal, your father will call you at 7:30 to discuss your schedule before the smoker. He's between dinners, so please keep it brief. Best, Denise.”
Above it in his phone, still, his father's texts from Tuesday night, and under them his own answer, two words he typed without deciding to:

msgs.text: Thursday. Brooks will collect you at 7:45.

blocks.text: On the bed, laid out like a police lineup:
One. His father's 1991 navy blazer, the Sigma Kappa Rho crest on the breast pocket in gold thread gone slightly green.
Two. The Rho quarter-zip Brooks handed him on the Quad last Wednesday. Legacies only. Fleece. It smells, faintly and permanently, of someone else's cologne.
Three. His own black sweater, the one with the hole at the cuff he's had since he was fifteen. The one Priya made him wear to callbacks because Konstantin would have a hole.
He wore the blazer Monday and Tuesday. It already knows his shoulders. It lies there on the bed with them still in it.
The blazer has been on the back of his door all week like someone waiting to be let in.
The voicemail he left his father on Monday is still unanswered. The blazer doesn't know that. The blazer looks optimistic.

The cleaners ticket is in his wallet, behind the Pruitt license. Lake water. 10/14/91. When he looks at the blazer his hand goes to the wallet through his jeans without asking him, the way you touch a bruise to see if it's still there.
The rush schedule, printed, on his desk. ATTIRE: FAMILY.
A knock that is somehow camp.
Simon Achterberg, camel coat, carrying a garment steamer like a crossbow.
Wardship protocol.
Friendship. Which is worse.
Friendship. Which is worse.
Friendship. Which is worse.
Your father's coat has been in a closet for thirty-five years. It smells like a senator's regret.
Raman told me. All of it. At lunch, over a salad she arranged and didn't eat. I've decided to be magnanimous. It's very slimming.
I've said everything I'm going to say about your floor. Twice. Once to Thorne, once to a dean's assistant who didn't ask.
Priya was very quiet at lunch. Is she ill? She's never quiet. I'm concerned. I'm also thrilled; I finished a sentence.
Simon sets the steamer down on the desk like a sacred object and looks at the bed. At the three of them. At Cal looking at the three of them.
His father told him which one. His father always tells him which one. That's the thing about his father: he's never once been unclear, from four hundred miles away, by text, through somebody else.

choices.label: ‘Simon. Make me look like my father.’

reaction.text: Simon's whole face lights up like a marquee in Times Square.
Finally. A ward with ambition.

He plugs in the steamer. It wheezes and starts to hiss, like Gerald's cousin from the city. He lifts the blazer off the bed by the shoulders, the way you'd lift a sleeping child out of a car, and hangs it on the closet door, and stands back to look at it with his head on one side.
Thirty-five years in a closet. I know the feeling. Stand back. This is going to get spiritual.

choices.label: The blazer. As told. ‘Got it.’

reaction.text: He puts it on without ceremony. It fits like it was waiting for him. It was.
Simon, a little disappointed to be unnecessary, steams the lapel anyway, “for the culture,” and looks at him in the mirror over the sink.
You look like a building.
He means it as a compliment. Cal hears the other thing.

choices.label: The quarter-zip. Brooks's uniform, not your father's.

reaction.text: Simon looks at the quarter-zip like it insulted his mother at a christening.
Bold. Brooks will love it. Your father will hear about it.

He steams it anyway, which is pointless, it's fleece; it just gets warm and smells more like the cologne. The blazer goes back into its tissue paper on the bed, gold crest up, watching the ceiling like a man lying in state.

choices.label: Your own sweater. Hole and all.

reaction.text: The family attire of a family of one.
He puts the steamer down. He doesn't joke for a full five seconds, which for Simon is a eulogy with bagpipes.
Then he picks a thread off the cuff, considers it, decides against it, and leaves the hole.
Keep it. It's the only thing you're wearing tonight that's yours.

blocks.text: INT. CAL'S SINGLE, THE MIRROR OVER THE SINK. DAY (THU 4:20 P.M.)
Simon steams the 1991 blazer on its hanger on the closet door with the solemnity of a priest and the commentary of a home-shopping host at two in the morning.

Wool from the before times. Lining: original. Note the hand-stitching at the shoulders: new, Boston, expensive, done by a man named Arturo who hates you personally. Buttons: horn. Real horn. Some animal died for your father's lapels, Calvin, and it died proud.
He turns the blazer in the steam like a rotisserie. He finds the crest with his thumb. He stays on it a second too long, the thumb moving over the gold thread, slowly, like reading Braille.
Then, too casually:
May I?
He doesn't wait. He takes off the camel coat and folds it over the chair, and puts on Richard Whitaker's 1991 Rho blazer.
It's big on him in the shoulders and exactly right in the length. He turns to the mirror over the sink, the mirror where Cal saw himself on Monday as the composite: second row, center, PLEDGE MASTER.
Simon tilts his jaw a few degrees. Then a few more. The way you'd match a face to a photo. He doesn't know Cal is watching him do it. Or he does, and he can't stop.
Cal has seen this angle before. Behind glass. On a wall in a hallway that smells like a museum that drinks.
Well.
A pause the length of a held breath.
Do I look like a Whitaker?
It's a joke question. He's asking it with his whole face.

choices.label: ‘You look like my father.’

reaction.text: Simon goes completely still in the mirror. Not the stillness of a joke landing. A different kind, the kind animals do.
Then the smile comes back, a beat late, like a train you've already given up on. He takes the blazer off quickly, the way you take off something hot.
Terrifying. I'll need a lie-down. And a Lillet. In that order, or simultaneously.
He holds it out to Cal by the hanger, at arm's length. His hand isn't quite steady. Cal notices. He has no idea why it would be.

choices.label: ‘You look like a man in a borrowed coat.’

reaction.text: All coats are borrowed, darling. Ask any poet. Ask any Achterberg.
He takes it off and smooths it on the hanger with real tenderness, the lapels, the cuffs, a hand flat on the back like you'd settle a child, and doesn't explain the second sentence.
Wear it well. Or don't. Wear it honestly, which I'm told is different.

choices.label: Take his photo in it.

reaction.text: Don't.
Then:
Actually, do.

He poses: chin up, three-quarter turn, the composite angle. For one frame he isn't posing at all. Cal looks at the photo on his phone: Simon in his father's coat, in his father's year, in his own bad mirror.
Simon reaches over and looks at it and doesn't delete it.
Send me that. For my files.
For his files. At the mailroom he told Cal he was building a file on his own father. Apparently it's catching.

blocks.text: INT. CAL'S SINGLE / EXT. THE QUAD TO ELM ROW. NIGHT (THU 7:30-7:58 P.M.)
7:30. He sits on the edge of the mattress, dressed, his phone face-up on his knee like a bomb with the timer off.
The blazer is buttoned. Then unbuttoned. Then buttoned. It looks right both ways, which is the problem with it.
The quarter-zip is zipped to the throat, like a man about to be fired into space.
His thumb finds the hole in his cuff and stays in it.
7:31. 7:36. 7:40. The phone does nothing. Phones are very good at that. They learn it from fathers.
He has a speech ready. He's had it ready since Tuesday at 4:58. It's three sentences long, and the second one is very good, and he's rehearsed it to Gerald twice. Gerald was unmoved.
7:45, exactly. Two knocks, the second softer, like a man checking a pulse.
Brooks Hadley in the doorway, in a navy suit that costs about what Dev's tuition costs, smiling the beautiful easy smile.
He sees the blazer and stops. One full second. For Brooks, that's a monologue.
That's his. From that year.
Bold. He said blazer.
Brooks looks at the hole in Cal's cuff for a long time, the way you'd look at a typo in a eulogy.
He'll hear.
Calvin. Your father's in a dinner. He asked me to have the talk.

They walk. Across the floodlit Quad, past the Commons steps and his grandfather's name, down the hill toward Elm Row and the black strip of the lake. Brooks delivers it like a man reading out a will he isn't in.

Econ 110 is where the boys who matter are. English is a hobby. Your seminar is, quote, “a woman with tenure and a grudge.” He'd like you to reconsider by the end of add/drop. Which, I'm aware, was Tuesday. He'd like you to reconsider anyway. He finds deadlines decorative.
He's pleased. He says you made the right call. Econ is where the boys who matter are. He'd like you to sit with them at lunch. He was specific about lunch.
He told me you texted him “No problem. I'm staying in English.” He read it to me. Twice. I think he admired the punctuation.
He told me you said it was a portal glitch. He knows it wasn't.
He told me you left him on read. He noticed. He notices everything.
Also, he mentioned the mailroom. Denise mentioned it to him. Everybody mentions everything to everybody. It's a very small family.
He mentioned the mailroom form. He was very calm about it. That's bad.
You promised him in August. He told me that too.
He says you're rushing. I'm choosing to believe him.
He says you're rushing. I'm choosing to believe him.
At the bottom of the hill, where the Rho's lights begin and the music starts coming up through the oaks, Brooks stops walking. He says the next part in a different voice. His own.
For what it's worth. Stay in English. He'll respect it in about thirty years. That's how long it takes him.
For what it's worth. I'd have stayed.
He rubs his left eyebrow with his thumb.
Cal sees it. It's his own tell, on somebody else's face, under somebody else's string lights. He doesn't know which sentence it was for.

choices.label: ‘Tell him I'm staying in English.’

reaction.text: I'll tell him. He'll hear it better from me. He usually does.
He says it lightly, like a joke about traffic, and walks on toward the music, and doesn't look back to see if it landed.

It landed. It's still landing, a little, three steps later, like a plane taxiing. His father will hear it. In Brooks's voice. With Brooks's pauses. Over a drink Cal will never be invited to, in a room Cal has never seen, and his father will nod at Brooks the way he has never once nodded at him.

choices.remember: Your father will hear about this.

choices.label: ‘You talk to him more than I do. You tell him.’

reaction.text: Brooks stops. For one second the smile isn't anywhere. It's just gone, like a light somebody forgot to pay for.
I'm his errand boy, Calvin. You're his son. Don't get them confused.
Then the smile comes back, too bright, and he takes Cal's arm above the elbow like an usher at a wedding.
Come on. You're going to be late to your own father's house.

choices.label: Call him. Right here, on the Quad.

reaction.text: DAD. It rings four times. Brooks stands two feet away with his hands in his pockets, not pretending not to listen.
“You've reached Richard Whitaker. Please leave a message with Denise.” The tone.
Dad. It's Cal. I'm staying in English. That's the whole talk.
He hangs up. Brooks lets out a low whistle, like a man watching a car he doesn't own go into a lake.
He'll keep that. He keeps everything.
He sounds almost proud. Of which one of them, Cal can't tell.

choices.remember: Your father has it on tape.

blocks.text: EXT. SIGMA KAPPA RHO, THE BACK LAWN. NIGHT (THU 8:00 P.M.)

Night one of rush is the joint Kappa-Rho smoker: the back lawn running down to the dock, string lights in the oaks, a bar under a tent, Kappa sisters hosting in pearls, and behind everything the lake, black and patient. The playlist is “September.” It is, in fact, the third of September. Somebody thinks that's very clever.
Fitz is at the gate in a pink tie, carding with a lacrosse stick.

blocks.name: FITZ
blocks.text: Tradition!
The freshman in front of Cal is big, blond and golden-retriever-shaped, and hands over a Vermont license with total confidence. AUGIE LINDQVIST, 18. From Minnesota.
Vermont. Like everybody.

blocks.name: FITZ
blocks.paren: admiringly, holding it up to the string lights
blocks.text: Dot's laminator!
Cal sees his own template in a stranger's hand, glossy as a diner menu.
Augie attaches himself to Cal instantly, like a big friendly dog to the one guest who looks like he knows where the food is.
Augie. My family makes combines. Like, the farm kind. Not the... other kind.
What's the other kind?
I don't know. I panicked.
At the bar two brothers are reciting his toast in Kennedy accents: “To my father, who couldn't be here!” Augie's eyes go wide.
Wait. That was YOU?
On the porch steps, HOLLIS PRESCOTT, 21, senior, Rho president. Square jaw, gentle voice, a senator's grandson, the face the Rho puts in its brochures. His welcome is so decent it's almost moving.
Brotherhood is the people who carry you home. That's all it is. Everything else is furniture.
His phone lights up in his hand with a single letter, S., and he turns it face-down mid-sentence, and finishes the sentence, and nobody but Cal sees the screen go dark.
Under the tent, at a card table, MARCUS BELL, 20, junior, rush chair, from Atlanta, a debater's perfect smile and a clipboard. He takes every rushee's name, hometown and 200-meter swim time.
Swim times?
Tradition. I keep records. Somebody in this house should.
That's a '91 cut. Single vent.
Vintage.

blocks.name: FITZ
blocks.text: Look at him. Already a brother!

blocks.paren: with real warmth, at the sweater
blocks.text: Thank God. A person.
Teddy Pemberton finds Cal immediately and stands as close as a man can stand without holding hands.

blocks.name: TEDDY
blocks.text: Thank God. Someone whose dad isn't on CNN.
By the bar, Margaux Vance is on Brooks's arm in pearls and navy. She doesn't look at Cal. She's had practice.
Then Tommy, late, in a borrowed blazer two sizes too small, arms flung wide like a man arriving at his own surprise party.
WHITAKER. We're brothers now!
This guy opened my door with a credit card. That's leadership.
Tommy is cool to him for the first ten minutes, sunglasses on at night, and then forgets to be, because he's Tommy.
Across the lawn, Brooks is watching Tommy. He writes something down.

choices.label: Work the president. Hollis.

reaction.text: Whitaker. Like the building.
Just Cal, I'm told. Brooks warned me.
He shakes Cal's hand like he's sorry about something. Then, quietly, the most honest thing anyone says all night:
The Rho is the best and worst thing that ever happened to me. Don't quote me. Your friend at the Herald would.
His phone lights again in his pocket; Cal sees the glow through the wool. Hollis doesn't take it out. For one second he looks like a man standing very still so a photograph won't blur.

choices.label: Work the rush chair. Marcus.

reaction.text: Why are you here? Not your father. You.
Cal gives him the charming answer. Marcus writes nothing. Cal gives him a truer one.
I said I would.
Marcus writes that down, word for word, and looks at it.
A man of his word. In this house that can get expensive.
He offers his hand. Dry, steady. His eyes go, once, to the smoke detector on the porch ceiling, and come back, and the smile never moves.

choices.label: Adopt the sidekick. Augie.

reaction.text: Can I stand next to you? You look like you know where the bathroom is.

Cal makes him laugh three times in five minutes and learns he's a farm-equipment heir from outside Duluth with a watch that's too good for his shoes and a laugh that's a little too loud for a man who isn't scared.
We should pledge together. Buddy system. My mom says never drink without a buddy.
Deal.
He'll remember that he said it.

blocks.text: INT. SIGMA KAPPA RHO, COMPOSITE HALLWAY AND CHAPTER ROOM. NIGHT (THU 9:00 P.M.)
Brooks taps a glass with a fork.
Legacies.

Eight freshmen peel off the lawn and follow him in through the composite hallway, past every class since 1891. Cal slows at 1991-92 without meaning to. His father, second row, center: PLEDGE MASTER. Brooks Hadley Jr. in the top row, happy. And in the bottom row, the faded green felt, the pried-off plate, T. C, and now, in his head, the alphabet. Carver. A dash. Cohen.
He has the oval in his camera roll and the slot in his head. He doesn't need to look. He looks.
He never photographed it. He doesn't need to. The dash on the roster has a face, and the face is empty.
The glass over the composite has been wiped. There isn't a speck on it. Somebody does this. Somebody he's never thought about once.

A brother's phone plays “O Fortuna” as they file into the chapter room, as a joke, and it's funny for about four bars. Long table. Candles. The silver loving cup. The founders in their frames, eight men who look like they'd sue you. Hollis at the head. Marcus with his clipboard. Brooks with the little leather notebook and the golf pencil.
No roasts tonight, Whitaker. You spent yours.
Marcus reads the swim times aloud from his clipboard like a man reading tide tables. When he gets to Cal, Brooks supplies it from the notebook without looking down.
Whitaker. Buoy and back. At night. Drunk. Two fifty-eight.
The brothers whistle. Somebody bangs the table.
Whitaker. Declined. Noted.
Whitaker. Declined. Noted.

blocks.name: FITZ
blocks.paren: to Brooks, delighted, about a week late
blocks.text: Regional manager at a boat dealership!
Brooks smiles and looks at Cal's clothes.
Your father's year. Recite.
Teddy Pemberton goes first. He gets halfway through his father's pledge class and freezes on a name, his mouth open.

blocks.name: A BROTHER
blocks.text: Ask your dad. Oh, wait. He's under oath.
The room laughs. Teddy looks at his shoes. Brooks lets the laugh go one second longer than he has to, and then one more, and then lifts a hand, and it stops.
Whitaker. Ninety-one.

Cal gives it to him. All thirty-four, the way Dev drilled them on the floor of the double with Yusuf timing. His father's year in his mouth like a prayer he didn't choose. Abernathy. Brandt. Carver, Paul.
Cal gives it to him, mostly. He hesitates once, because the last place he saw this list was on a corkboard in a basement.
The Herald's been asking the registrar about ninety-one. You wouldn't know anything about that.
You asked me by text. Ask me now.
And then?

Thirty brothers. Candlelight. The founders. Hollis polite, Marcus with his pen lifted. Brooks with the golf pencil resting on the page, waiting, like a man who already knows the answer and wants to hear how you'll say it.

choices.label: ‘Dash.’ Deadpan, like Dev taught you.

reaction.text: Dash.
A beat. Then the room laughs, the good laugh, the relief laugh. “Dash!” somebody shouts, and somebody else bangs the table. Hollis smiles. Marcus doesn't. Brooks writes something longer than a word.
Cohen, David.
He finishes. The brothers bang the table for him. Under the noise, Brooks, not smiling:
You say it like it's a guy.
It is a guy.
Brooks's thumb goes to his eyebrow.

choices.label: ‘The house ghost.’ His words, back at him.

reaction.text: The house ghost.

Brooks's own line, in his own chapter room. A few of the younger brothers laugh because it sounds like a joke. The older ones don't, because they've heard Brooks say it, in that hallway, to other freshmen.
Freshmen always ask. You didn't ask. You answered.
He writes.
Cohen, David.
Cal finishes. The table bangs. Brooks doesn't.
