reaction.text: T. C.
The room doesn't laugh. It doesn't do anything. Somebody's chair creaks, a long dry sound, like a boat.
Who's T. C.?
Marcus's pen stops on his clipboard. Then it moves.
Brooks looks at Cal for a long time across the candles, his face perfectly pleasant.
Next.
He points at Lindgren. On the way out, later, he passes behind Cal's chair and says, so quietly it might be the radiator:
Nobody says them out loud.

blocks.text: EXT. SIGMA KAPPA RHO, THE BACK LAWN BY THE DOCK STEPS. NIGHT (THU 9:40 P.M.)

Back on the lawn. Hollis's cousin's a cappella group is doing something to “September” that should be prosecuted in the Hague. Augie is trying to teach Tommy a Minnesota drinking song that turns out to be the Lord's Prayer.

Tommy has lost his borrowed blazer and found a Kappa's pearls, which he is wearing with great dignity. Teddy Pemberton is telling Fitz about his father's lawyers as if they're a band he's into. The whole lawn is lit and loud and smells like cut grass and money.
Margaux Vance has been on Brooks Hadley's arm all night. Navy and pearls, the campus's royal engagement, laughing at his jokes at exactly the correct volume, the way you'd tune a piano.
At 9:40 she takes her hand off his arm. She says something to him, close to his ear. His smile goes fixed, like a photograph of a smile.

Then she crosses the whole lawn. Past the bar. Past the Kappa sisters in their pearls. Past Hollis and Marcus and the string lights and the a cappella tragedy. In full view of everyone, in a straight line, the way you'd cross a stage. To Cal.
She stands next to him, close enough to be a statement. All over the lawn, phones come up like lighters at a concert.
Hello, Whitaker.
Then, for him:
Your photographer took the day off.
She's noticed the account went quiet. She's taking it as permission. Or she's taking it as an excuse. With her he can never tell, and it's the only time not being able to tell doesn't frighten him.
You chose homework over me yesterday. I'm choosing a lawn over you today. We're even.
I told you I changed my mind. This is what it looks like.
A Kappa sister passing with a tray of champagne sees him and lights up.

blocks.name: CAROLINE
blocks.text: Bookstore boy!
Bookstore's closed, Caroline.
She isn't wearing his parka. He can guess exactly where it is: on the back of her desk chair, two doors from the dormer, like a treaty nobody has signed.
She knows about the call. She's the only person on this whole lawn who does.
Before he can say anything she presses something small and cold into his palm, and closes his fingers over it. A nickel. Neither of them says anything about coins.
Across the lawn, Brooks lifts his glass to the two of them, slowly, all the way up, like a toast at a wedding he wasn't invited to.
The merger's off, he mouths. And drinks.

choices.label: Take her hand. In front of Brooks.

reaction.text: Her hand finds his before his finds hers. Fifty phones. Brooks's glass doesn't come down.
Twice in two days. People will talk.
That's the point, isn't it.

reaction.paren: very low, not looking at him, looking at the lawn like a jury
reaction.text: Now it's real. Now it's a picture.

She doesn't let go for a full minute. When she does, it's to straighten his collar, which is worse. It's a wife's gesture. She knows it. She does it anyway, slowly, both hands, with the whole lawn watching.

choices.label: Public and formal: ‘Hello, Vance.’

reaction.text: Hello, Vance.

He says it for the lawn and gives her the composite smile. She gives it back, perfect, a mirror. To anyone watching it's two legacies being civil at a smoker. To anyone standing next to them, it's two people trying very hard not to laugh.
Look at us. Our mothers would be so proud.
He doesn't know why she said mothers. He doesn't have one, to be proud. She didn't mean to say it. He can tell by how fast she drinks.

choices.label: Quietly: ‘Whose idea is this?’

reaction.text: Whose idea is this?
Mine.
You asked me that yesterday.
You gave the same answer.
It's still mine.
Then she looks out at the dark lake for a second too long.
Somebody has to decide something in my family. It might as well be me.

She takes a champagne off a passing tray and hands it to him, and doesn't take one for herself. She stays beside him until the song ends, not touching him, close enough that the lawn can't tell the difference. Then she goes back across the grass the way she came, in a straight line, and doesn't look at Brooks, which on this lawn is the loudest thing anyone has done all night.

blocks.text: INT. SIGMA KAPPA RHO, CHAPTER ROOM. NIGHT (THU 10:00 P.M.)
The legacies are called back in. The candles have burned down an inch. The founders haven't moved.
Hollis goes around the table handing each of them a cream card, heavy stock, the crest embossed so deep you can feel it from the back. I INTEND TO PLEDGE SIGMA KAPPA RHO. A line for a signature.

blocks.paren: kindly, like a doctor about a shot
blocks.text: It's not binding. It's a gentleman's word. Signed cards go in the cup.

The loving cup sits at the head of the table, silver, dented, older than the state of Massachusetts, which isn't true, but it looks it. Somebody has polished it today. The candlelight goes all the way around it and comes back.

Eight legacies. Eight cards. Down the table Hollis's pocket glows once through the wool, and he puts his hand over it without looking, like a man covering a cough. Out on the lawn the a cappella cousins have moved on to “Africa,” and the brothers at the door are singing along, and inside it is very quiet.
Lindgren signs before Hollis finishes the sentence. Teddy signs with his eyes shut, like he's jumping.

Brooks stands behind Cal's chair with a pen. Cal knows the pen: black lacquer, a gold band, the one in every photograph of Richard Whitaker signing something on the business channel. His father's pen, or one exactly like it. Brooks holds it out, cap off, over Cal's shoulder.
In this house a word is a contract.
Then, to Cal only, close:
You gave him yours in August.
You told him you'd think about it. He took that as yes.
You left him on read. He took that as yes too.
Marcus slides into the empty chair beside him and says, without moving his lips much:
Whatever you do with that card, do it on purpose.
Marcus, at the end of the table, just watches. He's very good at watching. It looks a lot like waiting.
Marcus, at the end of the table, just watches. He's very good at watching. It looks a lot like waiting.
His father's word. His father's pen. His father's house. His father's face in the hall outside, second row, center. And a line, with nothing on it yet, waiting for his name.

choices.label: Sign it. Put it in the cup.

reaction.text: CALVIN WHITAKER. In full. The same way he signed the placement essay. It looks the same on both. That's the strange part.
His hand starts a P. He turns it into a C. CALVIN WHITAKER. Nobody sees the P but him.
CALVIN WHITAKER, in full. His father's pen writes beautifully. Of course it does.

He drops the card into the loving cup. It makes almost no sound. The brothers bang the table anyway, and Fitz yells “LEGACY!” from the doorway, and Brooks puts a hand on his shoulder: warm, brief, proprietary, exactly where his father's hand would go, if his father were the kind of man whose hand went anywhere.
At 10:31 p.m., his phone:
At the door Brooks adds the rest, to the room: times at the dock at eleven-thirty. Voluntary. Brothers are welcome to watch.
He has counted every one of those in his life. He adds this one to the count. It doesn't feel like he thought it would. It feels like a receipt.

choices.label: Pocket it, unsigned. ‘I'll sleep on it.’

reaction.text: He folds the card once and puts it inside his jacket, against his wallet, against the cleaners ticket behind the Pruitt license.
I'll sleep on it.
The room doesn't quite know what to do with that. Somebody laughs and then stops.
That's allowed.
Of course it is.
The pen goes back into Brooks's pocket. He doesn't stop smiling.
Sleep on it down at the dock, then. Times are at eleven-thirty. Legacies and the ones who are thinking.
At 10:31 p.m., his phone:

choices.label: Put the pen down. Stand up. Walk out.

reaction.text: He takes the pen from Brooks, and puts it down on the table, parallel to the card, the way he squared Priya's pages in the printer tray. He stands.

Thirty brothers watch him do it. Nobody says anything, because nobody has ever done it on night one, and there isn't a tradition for it, and in this house if there isn't a tradition for it, it isn't happening.
He left his father a voicemail two hours ago on the Quad. This is the rest of the message.

He walks out through the composite hallway past his father's face, in his father's coat. His father's coat walking out of his father's house. He doesn't look at the empty oval. He feels it look at him.
He walks out through the composite hallway past his father's face, in their fleece, zipped to the throat. He doesn't look at the empty oval. He feels it look at him.

He walks out through the composite hallway past his father's face. He doesn't look at the empty oval. He feels it look at him. The hole in his cuff catches on the front-door handle, and for one second the house holds onto him by a thread.
The front door of the Rho is heavier than it looked. Most of them are.

choices.remember: Your father will hear about this.

blocks.text: Act Three · Times
EXT. THE RHO DOCK, TAMSIN LAKE. NIGHT (THU 11:30 P.M.)

The gray boards. The bare bulb on its post, ticking with moths. The white buoy a hundred yards out, just a pale thought on the black. Across the water, the boathouse light, small and steady, like someone on the far shore who has been keeping watch for a very long time.

Twelve rushees in good clothes on a dock at night. Brooks with a stopwatch and the little leather notebook. Marcus with his clipboard, not writing anything, watching everything. Up the lawn the house is lit like a liner, and the music comes down the grass to the water and stops there, as if it isn't allowed any farther.
Somebody has brought a bottle. Somebody always has. It goes down the line of rushees hand to hand like a collection plate, and everyone drinks from it, because everyone else did.
He's swum to that buoy at night. He knows it's farther than it looks. Everything out here is.
He's stood on these boards before and said no. He's never been in this water.
He's stood on these boards before and said no. He's never been in this water.

blocks.paren: to Cal, as they come down the lawn
blocks.text: Thinking men get to watch.

blocks.paren: to Cal, as they come down the lawn
blocks.text: Brothers get to watch.
Nobody has to swim. Times are voluntary. Legacies have theirs already.
He looks at Cal when he says it. Which is how you get everyone to swim.
Tommy Reyes, three beers and one hit to the head into his night, is already pulling off his shirt over the Kappa's pearls, then one shoe, hopping.
Like a Labrador! All heart! No form!
There's two of the clock sometimes. Cal hears it again, now, in Tommy's voice, under the music still coming down from the house.
You gonna get me benched from the lake too, Whitaker?
Is this safe?
It's tradition.

blocks.paren: at Cal's elbow, not letting go of his sleeve
blocks.text: Buddy system.
Augie hangs back by Marcus, holding his own shoes against his chest like a man at a funeral.
Augie hangs back by Marcus, holding his own shoes against his chest like a man at a funeral.
Tommy dives. Clean, loud, laughing in the air.
Tommy dives. Clean, loud, laughing in the air.
Tommy dives yelling “WORCESTER'S FINEST!” and hits the water still yelling it.

Brooks clicks the stopwatch. The flashlight finds him. Strong, wild strokes toward the buoy, a rooster tail of white, the rushees cheering like it's the Olympics. Then a stroke that goes nowhere. Then another.
He stops ten yards short of the buoy. Treads water. Turns his head one way, then the other, slowly, like he's looking for something he put down a minute ago and can't think where.
The beam on him starts to shake.

choices.label: Go in after him.

reaction.text: Shoes off, jacket on the boards, and he's in. The cold like a slap from someone who loves you. The water he knows.
Shoes off, jacket on the boards, and he's in. The cold like a slap. It's his first time in this water and it takes the air out of him like a fist.
He reaches Tommy in a dozen strokes. Tommy is laughing, spitting, blinking at him like they've run into each other in a supermarket.
It keeps moving, bro. The buoy. It won't hold still.
Cal takes Tommy's hand and puts it on the buoy. They hang there together, breathing, the dock a little yellow island behind them, the rushees cheering like it was a race and somebody won.
Don't tell coach.
He lays his cheek against the buoy like a pillow, and closes his eyes, and Cal holds onto both of them, the buoy and the boy, until his own legs stop shaking.

choices.label: Call him back from the dock: ‘Reyes! Back! Now!’

reaction.text: REYES. Back. Now.
It comes out in a voice Cal didn't know he had. The voice of a man who expects to be obeyed. His father's voice, on the phone, from four hundred miles away.

Tommy turns instantly, like a dog called by its name, and swims back, slow and crooked, and Cal kneels on the boards and hauls him up by both wrists. Tommy lies on his back on the dock, streaming, laughing at the stars.
You sound like my dad.
He's still laughing when he says it. Then he stops laughing.

choices.label: Stand beside Brooks. Watch the light.

reaction.text: He steps up next to Brooks. Up close, the hand on the stopwatch is white at the knuckles and the flashlight is jittering like a moth against a window.
Brooks isn't looking at Tommy. He's looking at the water around Tommy. At the black. The way you'd look at a dog that bit you once.
His breathing is counted. Four in. Hold. Cal hears it, under the cheering. He doesn't know what it means. He only knows where he has read it before: carved low in a wainscot on the fourth floor.
Out on the water Tommy finds the buoy on his own, slaps it, whoops. The rushees roar. Brooks's light steadies, all at once, like a hand being taken off it.
You didn't see that.

blocks.text: EXT. THE RHO DOCK, AFTER. NIGHT (FRI 12:20 A.M.)

The rushees have gone up to the house with Tommy wrapped in a Rho towel between Augie and Marcus, Tommy singing, Augie singing along to a different song. Brooks and Cal are alone on the boards. The bulb ticks.
Brooks sits on the edge with his shoes off and his feet over the water. Not in it. An inch above it. He pours two fingers of something brown into two Solo cups and holds one up without looking.
You didn't see that.
It sits between them for the rest of the night, the thing Cal didn't see.
You went in after him. Nobody goes in after anybody. That's the first thing they teach you.
You've got his voice. When you want it.

Cal sits. He takes the cup. It's bourbon, and it's good, and it's his father's brand, the one on the bar cart in Boston that nobody else is allowed to open. He doesn't say so. Brooks watches him not say so.
He sends the house a case every Christmas. With a card. The card says “Brothers.” Typed. Denise types it.
Your father stood right here. I've told you that.
You've told me.
I'll keep telling you. It's the only thing about him I'm sure of.
Brooks reaches over and taps the unsigned card through Cal's jacket with one finger, like knocking on a door to see if anyone's home.
Sleep on it. I don't.

blocks.paren: once, lightly, like trying a word on in a mirror
blocks.text: Brother.
Up at the house someone has put on “Fortunate Son” again, the third time tonight. Brooks hums two bars of it, badly, and stops, as if he's caught himself doing something in public.
He drinks. The lake is perfectly still, as if nothing has ever happened in it. As if it has never once in its life been asked to keep anything.
Brooks's thumb finds his left eyebrow and stays there. He doesn't seem to know it's there. He's looking at the buoy. Cal's looking at him.
He's almost saying something. Cal has read people for a living since he was eleven, and he's never seen anyone stand this close to the edge of a sentence.

choices.label: ‘Who was T. C.?’

reaction.text: Who was T. C.?
You said the letters in my chapter room. Now you want the rest.
Brooks smiles at the water.
A boy who couldn't swim.
A long beat. The bulb ticks.
Joking.
The thumb on the eyebrow. He finishes his cup.
Ask your father. I'd love to hear what he says. Tell me after. Tell me word for word.
He stands, pats Cal's shoulder, and goes up the lawn barefoot, carrying his shoes, like a boy coming in from summer.

choices.label: ‘Do you ever actually sleep, Hadley?’

reaction.text: Brooks laughs. Really laughs. The laugh Margaux said was his father's.
With the lights on.
He says it as a joke, and it isn't one, and Cal can't know that.
Every light. Like a hospital. Like a gas station on the Pike at four in the morning.
He looks at Cal sideways.
Don't make that face. You've got your three a.m. too. Everyone on Instagram's seen it.

choices.label: ‘Tell my father yourself. You talk to him more than I do.’

reaction.text: The second time tonight. Brooks doesn't stop smiling.
I text him. He reads it. Sometimes at two-thirty in the morning. Sometimes he answers.
He swirls his cup and watches the brown go round.
You get “Proud of you.” I get “Good.” That's the whole difference between us, Calvin. Two words.

He gets up. He leaves the bottle. He doesn't look back, and he doesn't put his shoes on, and the boards are wet, and he walks up them like a man who has walked up wet boards in the dark many, many times.

blocks.text: Act Three · Times
EXT. SIGMA KAPPA RHO, FRONT PORCH / ELM ROW. NIGHT (THU 10:05 P.M.)

The front door shuts behind him on thirty brothers and a loving cup. Elm Row: string lights, a girl crying happily on the Kappa steps across the street, a boy throwing up neatly into a hydrangea, the lake behind the houses like a held breath.
He's three steps down when the door opens again.

Brooks. Alone. No drink. One hand in his pocket. In the other, a cream card, unsigned, picked up off the table where Cal left it, held between two fingers like something you'd return to a lost and found.
Nobody walks out the first night.
They walk back in. Usually by the third.

He comes down one step. Behind him, through the open door, the house is already moving on: somebody laughing, somebody shouting for ice, the a cappella cousins starting “Africa” on the lawn. Nobody has come to the door but Brooks. Nobody else will.
He comes down another step.
Your father walked out once. Junior year. He came back the next morning and they made him pledge master.
He says it like a fact. He says it like a man who has read it somewhere, in somebody's handwriting. There's no way for Cal to check it. There never is, with Brooks.
I told him you're staying in English. I'll tell him this too. He's going to think I'm a bad influence.

Across the street, on the Kappa porch, Margaux Vance has seen the whole thing. The girl who held his hand on the lawn half an hour ago. She lifts her glass, and then she sets it down on the railing, carefully, like she's changed her mind about what it means.
Across the street, on the Kappa porch, Margaux Vance has seen the whole thing. She doesn't come over. She lifts her glass an inch, which could mean anything. With her it usually means three things.
Across the street, on the Kappa porch, Margaux Vance has seen the whole thing. She doesn't come over. She lifts her glass an inch, which could mean anything. With her it usually means three things.
His father's coat is on his back. The man who wants it most is holding his card.
Their fleece is still zipped to his throat. The man who wants it most is holding his card.
Nothing he's wearing is theirs. The only thing of theirs out here is the card in Brooks's hand.
His father's fraternity brother's son, or whatever Brooks is to all of this, standing on his father's steps, holding the door back open.

choices.label: ‘Tell him I'll discuss it with him. In person.’

reaction.text: Tell him I'll discuss it with him. In person.

reaction.paren: like a word in a language he studied once
reaction.text: In person.
That'll be new for both of you.
He nods.
Trustee Weekend. He'll be here. I'll tell him you said so.
He goes back up the steps. At the door he turns.
Calvin. You'll still get a bid. You know that. He'll make sure.
The door shuts. It sounds like a safe.

He stands on the bottom step with his hands in his pockets. In person. He has never once in his life discussed anything with his father in person. He's not sure he knows how. He's not sure his father does.

choices.label: Hold it out to him: ‘You want it more than I do.’

reaction.text: He takes the blazer off on the steps and holds it out. Brooks looks at it for a long time. Then he takes it, carefully, like it's wet, and doesn't put it on, and doesn't hand it back.
You don't know what you're giving away.

It isn't a threat. It's almost pity. He goes inside with the coat over his arm. Through the tall front windows Cal watches him stop in the composite hallway and put it on, and stand there in front of 1991 in Richard Whitaker's coat, very still, like a man waiting for a photograph to be taken.
He unzips the quarter-zip on the steps and holds it out. Legacies only. Brooks takes it and doesn't put it on.
Legacies only. I'll give it to a legacy.

He goes inside. He doesn't look back. He holds the fleece against his chest like something rescued from a fire, and the door shuts on it, and Cal stands on the steps in his shirtsleeves in September, lighter by exactly one fleece, which turns out to be quite a lot.
He takes the card out of Brooks's fingers and holds it out to him.
You sign it.
Brooks looks at it for a long time. Then he folds it, once, and puts it in his own breast pocket, over his heart.
I did. Two years ago. Nobody asked me to.
He goes back inside with his hand flat over the pocket, like a man keeping a letter from getting wet, and the door closes behind him on the music.

choices.label: Say nothing. Walk down Elm Row without looking back.

reaction.text: He walks. Brooks doesn't call after him.
Elm Row is long. The string lights end before it does. Halfway down, past the hydrangea and the boy and the girl still crying happily, he looks back once.
Brooks is still on the steps, hands in his pockets, the card in one of them, watching him go the way you'd watch a boat you used to own leave the harbor with somebody else at the wheel.
On the Kappa porch, Margaux has gone inside. Her glass is on the railing. Full.

blocks.text: INT. FENNIMORE LIBRARY, CIRCULATION DESK. NIGHT (THU 11:00 P.M.)
Fennimore at eleven. The reading-room lamps in long green rows, three exhausted pre-meds asleep on their organic chemistry, the tower bells somewhere above saying the hour like they're tired of it.

He came here because it's open and it isn't Lowell and it isn't Elm Row and it doesn't have anybody's name on it that he's related to. He walked the whole way with his hands in his pockets and his phone face-down in one of them, waiting for it to buzz. It didn't. That's its own kind of message. He's fluent.
He's in shirtsleeves in September at eleven at night.
He's in shirtsleeves in September at eleven at night.
Behind the circulation desk, scanning returns with a beep every four seconds, in a FENNIMORE STAFF lanyard: Nora Castellanos.
She never told him she works here. She sees him. His face. His clothes. The time.
Beep.
No comment, I assume.
Are you here as a source or a patron.
Are you here as a source or a patron.
Twenty-five hours a week. Don't make it a thing, Whitaker. I'm not a thing.
Beep.
You look like you just walked out of somewhere.
He doesn't say where. She doesn't ask. She checks out a book to nobody and slides it across the desk to him, a library copy of something, it doesn't matter what, a reason to stand there.
Where's your jacket.
I gave it away.
To who.
To the guy who wanted it.
You said you wouldn't read under it. I believed you. Don't make me regret it.
You asked what was under the bars. Still no.
Three coats. Still.
You have nine minutes until I close the stacks. Use them or don't.

Behind her, on the cart of returns, a stack of Herald back issues, rubber-banded, waiting to be shelved in a basement nobody visits. The top one is from Monday. THE WHITAKER PROBLEM. She sees him see it and puts her coffee down on top of his name.
Beep. Beep. The first person who sees him after he walked out of his father's house is the person who wrote THE WHITAKER PROBLEM. He thinks that's probably right. He thinks she'd think so too.

choices.label: ‘I walked out of my father's house tonight.’

reaction.text: Beep. She stops scanning.
She looks at him the way she looked at him in Marsh's room when he said his first lie: like a person and not a quote.
On night one.
In front of everyone.
You called your father once when you were eleven. Tonight you didn't. That's a pattern, Whitaker. Writers love a pattern.
She puts the scanner down.
Okay. That's off the record, Whitaker. Not for print. Just for me.
She writes nothing down. It's the first time he has ever seen her not write something down.

choices.label: ‘You work here? Since when?’

reaction.text: Since August twentieth. Before you moved in. Before your toast.
Beep.
Scholarships cover tuition. Not the rest. The rest is me.
Don't buy me a coffee about it.
I wasn't going to.
You were thinking about it. Your face does a thing. Like you're reaching for your wallet.
He was. He leaves it in his pocket. She sees that too, and the corner of her mouth goes, just the corner, like a page turning in a draft.

choices.label: Take out the cleaners ticket. ‘What does this mean to you?’

reaction.text: He takes the ticket out of his wallet, from behind the Pruitt license, and lays it on the desk between two returns. Yellowed. Soft as a moth wing. ALDER FALLS CLEANERS · RUSH · 10/14/91 · NAVY BLAZER · STAIN: lake water.
What does this mean to you?
Nora doesn't touch it. She doesn't do anything at all. The scanner in her hand beeps once, on its own, at nothing.
Where did you get this.
My father's blazer. The inside pocket.
A long silence. Somewhere above them the tower bells start the quarter hour and think better of it.
Can I photograph it?

He nods. She does, twice, flat on the desk, like evidence, her hand perfectly steady and her face perfectly still, and slides it back to him with one finger, the way you'd push something back across a table at a poker game.
